question: Why do healthcare workers use a standard system for naming medicines?

options.A: To help patients memorize foreign languages
options.B: To make drug manufacturing more expensive
options.C: To ensure clear communication among health workers
options.D: To hide the true chemical makeup of a medicine

explanation: A standardized naming system allows midwives, doctors, and pharmacists to discuss treatments accurately without confusion. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why do most medicines have more than one name?

options.A: Midwives prefer using complex chemical terms only
options.B: Local herbs do not have official scientific titles
options.C: The government changes the name every single year
options.D: Different companies and scientists use different naming systems

explanation: A single medicine often gets a chemical description, an official non-proprietary name, and various brand names depending on the manufacturer. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h1)

question: What does a drug's chemical name tell you about it?

options.A: The commercial price set by the pharmacy
options.B: The country where the drug was manufactured
options.C: Which disease the medicine treats best
options.D: Its exact atomic and molecular structure

explanation: Chemical names spell out the precise chemical building blocks and arrangement of atoms within the drug molecule. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h2)

question: Why do midwives avoid using chemical names during daily ward rounds?

options.A: The Nursing and Midwifery Council forbids speaking chemistry
options.B: Patients refuse to take drugs with chemical titles
options.C: Chemical names only apply to traditional herbal remedies
options.D: They are far too long and complicated to speak easily

explanation: Because chemical names describe complex molecular structures, they are impractical for fast-paced clinical communication and prescription writing. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h2)

question: Who usually assigns the official generic name to a new drug?

options.A: Patient advocacy groups in local communities
options.B: The local patent office in each individual state
options.C: International bodies like the World Health Organization

explanation: Global organizations coordinate to give drugs clear, non-proprietary generic names that remain consistent worldwide. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h3)

question: How does knowing drug name endings (stems) help a midwife in practice?

options.A: It helps identify the drug class and general function quickly
options.B: It tells the exact financial cost of the medication
options.C: It guarantees the medication will be completely free of side effects
options.D: It allows the midwife to manufacture the drug at home

explanation: Recognizing common suffixes lets clinicians deduce how an unfamiliar drug works based on its generic name ending. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h3)

question: What is another common term for a proprietary drug name?
explanation: Proprietary names are commercial brand names created and registered by individual pharmaceutical companies. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h4)

question: Why might a single generic medicine be sold under many different brand names?

options.A: The chemical structure changes every time a new factory opens
options.B: Hospitals require a new brand name for every patient admitted
options.C: Multiple competing companies manufacture and market their own versions
options.D: Government regulations forbid using the same name twice

explanation: Once a drug's patent protection expires, various pharmaceutical firms can produce it and give it their own unique trade names. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h4)

question: Which type of drug name is controlled directly by the pharmaceutical company that makes it?
explanation: Commercial manufacturers create and trademark proprietary names to market their specific products. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h5)

question: What should a midwife do when the hospital changes the brand of a commonly used drug?

options.A: Throw away all the old stock immediately without checking
options.B: Check the generic name to confirm the active ingredient is identical
options.C: Assume the new drug is completely unrelated and dangerous
options.D: Refuse to administer any medication that has a colorful wrapper

explanation: Looking at the generic name ensures the active drug substance is correct, regardless of what commercial brand name is printed on the new box. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h5)

question: What does the safety acronym LASA stand for in pharmacology?
explanation: LASA refers to drug names that are easily confused visually or verbally, which is a major cause of clinical medication errors. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h6)

question: How does tall-man lettering help prevent medication errors on the ward?

options.A: It uses capital letters to highlight the differing parts of similar drug names
options.B: It automatically calculates the correct dosage for pregnant women
options.C: It ensures that only senior doctors are allowed to write dangerous drugs
options.D: It prints prescription orders in giant fonts for nurses with poor eyesight

explanation: By capitalizing specific syllables in look-alike drug names, tall-man lettering draws the eye to what makes the two medications distinct. [learn more](BMP124_U1_T2#BMP124_U1_T2_h6)
